chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Carney's classical riffs and Gunable's mouthpiece training
summary: McRae recalls Carney's technical control and returns to Gunable's lessons on embouchure, saying Foots Thomas wanted to teach him.

And just before he comes out, he goes into a technical thing, like a cello player (singing notes). He's playing classics. He's not playing the arrangements. He goes into a classic thing, you know. A classic riffs. Just like he's playing (singing notes), and goes right into (singing notes), back into the jazz again. All of a sudden he's into a classic field. He's playing a classic thing. See, this is one thing that I tried to learn that Mack Venable taught me when I was teaching with him -- studying with him in Philly.
He tell me to come to practice Sunday afternoon and just bring your mouthpiece. See, just playing the horn is not all. It's what you do with that mouthpiece.
And the control of your muscles -- from your jaws down. You can play without even dropping this jaw.
Your face will stay the same, I don't care what you got to do. It takes all the pressure off your neck when you develop these muscles in here.
Muscles from the lower lip down?
You can go from the high note to the bottom note. You

Those are the things that -- People wonder -- musicians wonder how can a guy do this. How's that. Because they have studied to learn how to do that. They developed themselves. They had good teachers. A good teacher can bring out a lot of things in you. You may have a lot of things in you that you don't know yourself. He can bring them out. A good teacher can help you. If you got the -- Like Foots Thomas always told me, he say, "Why don't you study with me just six months so I can just say that you studied with me?" And that would mean a lot to him. That would mean a lot to his pupils. "Oh, Teddy McRae studied with you, so and so studied with you?" You know, (inaudible).
